newsitem.title: USA: NYNEX unit loses ruling on info providers.
newsitem.headline: NYNEX unit loses ruling on info providers.

text.p: A state administrative law judge ruled in favor of a group of companies that sell telephone information services in a case involving New York Telephone Co, a NYNEX Corp unit, the group said on Wednesday.

The companies, which provide sports and financial news, weather, horoscopes and other information through phone numbers beginning with 976, said the judge recommended a damage award of between $40 million and $50 million be paid to them.

Public Service Commission Administrative Law Judge Frank Robinson found that New York Telephone engaged in "gross negligence and willful misconduct," including a cover-up in the legal proceedings, according to a statement by the group.

The companies that issued the statement are Accurate Info Ltd, Statistical Phone Information Services and Phone Programs Inc. Tom Butler, a spokesman for Phone Programs, said the three are major players in the so-called "mass announcement services" business.
Through New York Telephone, the vendors sell information via brief messages at a charge of 40 cents a call. Fifty percent of the charge goes to the vendor and the rest to New York Telephone.

The vendors complained that when New York Telephone replaced certain equipment and software in 1990, problems developed with their services. Many callers could not gain access to the programs and instead heard busy signals or their phones went dead, the vendors said, alleging they lost business as a result.
New York Telephone spokesman Steve Marcus said the company "strongly disagrees" with Robinson's recommendations and comments.
He said the company would file a brief in the first week of February seeking a full review of Robinson's ruling by Public Service Commission, a New York state regulatory body.
Marcus said Robinson's recommendations were "fundamentally flawed." He said the company acted responsibly in putting up a digital switch to process calls to information services.
The company also acted promptly to resolve any problems that arose from the installation of the new equipment, he said.
The vendors said Robinson has proposed a formula estimated to result in $25.2 million in refunds, representing lost business to them.
In addition, Robinson also found that New York Telephone reneged on a requirement that it assume some of the cost to advertise and promote the providers' networks, they said.
That, plus the estimated lost business, could result in refunds of between $40 million and $50 million, they said.
They said Robinson was also critical of New York Telephone's dismissal of its 976 product manager, who allegedly corroborated many of the allegations against the company.
